q: A firstborn is redeemed with a cloth worth less than five *sela*. When is the son redeemed?
options: When the priest himself values it at five *sela*, as Rav Kahana did
Never: it must be worth five *sela* on the market
Always, if the father says it is worth five
Only with a formal appraisal
why: Rav Kahana said, "For me, this cloth is worth five *sela*." Rav Ashi limits this to a great man who needs a head cloth.

q: 'Be betrothed to me with a hundred dinars,' and he gave her one. What does R. Elazar rule?
options: Betrothed now; he must complete the payment
Not betrothed until all hundred are given
Not betrothed at all
Betrothed only if she agrees again
why: The hundred works as a condition (*al menat*), and whoever says 'on condition' is as if he said 'from now'.

q: He is counting out a hundred dinars for betrothal. Until when may either side retract?
options: Until the last dinar is given
Until the first dinar is given
Until half is given
Neither may retract once he begins
why: Either because he said 'this hundred', or (Rav Ashi) because when he counts she expects the whole sum.

q: 'With this hundred,' and one of the dinars turned out to be a worn silver dinar that can be spent with difficulty. What is the law?
options: Betrothed, and he must exchange it
Not betrothed
Doubtfully betrothed
Betrothed, and he owes nothing
why: It is still a silver dinar. A copper coin she didn't notice, or one dinar short, means she is not betrothed.

q: He promised her a hundred and gave her his own *mashkon* (collateral) instead. Is she betrothed (Rav Nachman)?
options: No: the hundred wasn't given, and a *mashkon* is only security
Yes, the *mashkon* is worth money
Yes, if it is worth a hundred
Only if she keeps it
why: "No hundred here, no *mashkon* here." A creditor holding another person's *mashkon* is different: he owns it in part (R. Yitzchak), so he can betroth with it.

q: She takes the betrothal money and throws it into the sea. Is she betrothed?
options: No, though she must repay him
Yes: she accepted it first
Yes, if she meant to test his temper
Only if witnesses saw her take it
why: Destroying it is a rejection, even though she owes him its value.

q: She says, 'Give it to my father, on condition that he accepts it for me.' Is she betrothed?
options: Yes: her father becomes her agent
No: it's a gift to her father
Only if her father is present
No, only a stranger can be her agent
why: Without the condition, 'give it to my father' is no betrothal; with it, the receiver acts for her (even a stranger).

q: 'Be betrothed to me with this loaf,' and she says, 'Give it to the dog.' When is she betrothed?
options: If the dog is hers
Never
Always
Only if the dog was chasing her
why: Her own dog benefits her. A dog chasing her is *teiku*: perhaps rescue is a benefit, or perhaps he was obliged to save her anyway.
